source.title: Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models
source.authors: Song Bian; Ming-Hao Yan; Shivaram Venkataraman

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some extracted text is garbled, but the relevant sections, tables, and figures are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains language models, fits loss-scaling curves, and evaluates predictions on larger runs, using loss measurements similar to the original scaling-law work. It also extends the fitted law with an architecture term.
record.gate_note: The study reports loss-scaling fits and prediction results, fit sensitivity to training data and model-shape selection, and accuracy-versus-loss plots. Latency and throughput results, and downstream evaluations of Morph-1B against other pretrained models, are not rows because they do not measure the versions' scaling or prediction claims. Related-work descriptions of other papers are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The authors train 63 decoder-only LMs (80M–339M for fitting, plus 1B tests) and fit Chinchilla-form loss laws to smoothed training loss. They check prediction on held-out 1B and over-trained runs and vary the fit data and shape selection. This bears on V1, V2 and V7 directly, and on V4 and V6 through figures.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that model shape strongly affects inference latency and that adding an aspect-ratio term to the Chinchilla law makes loss prediction more accurate and robust. They find over-training data essential for fitting, and that downstream accuracy is hard to predict from loss, so they rank candidates and evaluate them. Morph-1B, a wider and shallower model, cuts latency 1.8× at similar accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits a Chinchilla-style loss function to its own decoder-only language-model runs, adding an aspect-ratio term for its inference-efficient law. It uses Levenberg–Marquardt least-squares fitting and sets the relevant exponents equal to simplify fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction performance changes when over-training data is excluded and when model shapes are selected randomly. The fitted α values also differ across the reported fit setups.

fits_no_version.finding: The shape-augmented law ranks the loss of aspect-ratio variants at 1B perfectly (Spearman 1.00). The Chinchilla form gives -0.40, and 0.80 vs 0.40 without over-training data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, aspect ratio produces systematic, predictable loss differences that a size-only law misses.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The scaling-law fitting runs are mostly small: the paper describes fitting with models from 80M to 339M parameters, with evaluation of larger models including 1B. The authors state they could not scale training to 7B models. Loss is smoothed training loss used as an estimate of test loss, not direct held-out cross-entropy. Several architecture-loss and downstream accuracy results are presented as plots without numerical values; no error bars or confidence intervals are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported results were left out. Architecture-loss plots are included as figure-only rows because the paper does not give numerical values for the plotted points.

untested.parts: Held-out cross-entropy (the study uses smoothed training loss). A separate compute power law. Ranges beyond about 80M–1B parameters and 1.6B–30B tokens.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude; the tested gap is about 3× in parameters and roughly 10× in compute.
Not tested: no compute-optimal allocation is fitted.
The magnitude of loss change with shape is not reported numerically; the plots are figure-only.
Only three task plots, with no quantified fit.

missing.what: Implied magnitude of the shape effect. With ε≈0.0011–0.0016 and γ=α≈0.6, the factor (1+εR^γ) changes loss by roughly 0.5–5% over R≈16–512. This is my own calculation, not stated by the authors, but it is relevant to V4.
Repeat random-shape trials. Chinchilla MSE is 0.0096 and 0.0091 (R² 0.969, 0.971) vs inference-efficient MSE 0.0019 and 0.0011.
The Chinchilla fit without over-training data has a negative A coefficient (-25287.67), an implausible fit.

record.verdict_notes: The fitting range is small (80M–339M) and the prediction target is 1B, so V2 is tested only over about 3× in parameters. Loss is smoothed training loss. The exponents α, β and γ are tied equal by construction, which limits what the α values say about V3/V7 exponent splits. Spearman rows were relinked to none because they rank shape variants rather than extrapolate scale. R15 and R16 are erroneous or duplicate. No error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses smoothed training loss to estimate test loss; it does not report held-out cross-entropy directly. It tests parameter and token variation, not a separate power law in training compute.
The reported scaled-up loss prediction is for 1B models, not runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting models; no larger-scale extrapolation is tested.
The study does not optimize parameter and token allocation under a fixed compute budget or fit their compute-optimal growth trends.
Loss is plotted across aspect ratios, but the paper does not state the individual loss values or quantify whether architecture changes loss only slightly.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
The study plots accuracy against loss for PIQA, BoolQ, and HellaSwag only; it does not establish a general downstream scaling law across tasks or models.
The study tests dependence on over-training data and model-shape selection. It does not test whether curves systematically bend away from a single power law across broader scales or setups.
